content: 1. Patients with CD4 cell counts below 50 cells/mm³ should initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) within the first two weeks of starting tuberculosis (TB) treatment. This recommendation is based on expert opinion and is supported by high certainty of evidence. 2. For patients with tuberculous meningitis, an initial adjuvant corticosteroid therapy using dexamethasone or prednisolone, tapered over 6–8 weeks, is strongly recommended. This recommendation is supported by moderate certainty of evidence. 3. In cases of tuberculous pericarditis, adjuvant corticosteroid therapy may be considered. However, this is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 4. To improve adherence to TB treatment, one or more of the following interventions may be offered to patients or healthcare providers: Use of a tracer or digital medication monitor (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Provision of material support to patients (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). Psychological support for patients (conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). Education and training for healthcare staff (conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 5. Communityor home-based treatment support is recommended over health facility-based or unsupervised treatment for patients on TB therapy. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 6. Treatment support provided by trained lay providers or healthcare workers is preferred over support administered by family members or unsupervised treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 7. Video-supported treatment can replace in-person treatment observation if video communication technology is available and can be appropriately organized and managed by healthcare providers and patients. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 8. Patients with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) should primarily receive ambulatory care rather than care models based on hospitalization. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 9. A decentralized model of care is recommended over a centralized model for patients undergoing MDR-TB treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 10. For children with TB, the following daily dosages of anti-TB medications are recommended: Isoniazid (H): 10 mg/kg (range 7–15 mg/kg), maximum dose 300 mg/day. Rifampicin (R): 15 mg/kg (range 10–20 mg/kg), maximum dose 600 mg/day. Pyrazinamide (Z): 35 mg/kg (range 30–40 mg/kg). Ethambutol (E): 20 mg/kg (range 15–25 mg/kg). This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 11. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis in settings with low HIV prevalence and low isoniazid resistance, and who are HIV-negative, can be treated with a three-drug regimen (HRZ) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for four months. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 12. Children with extensive pulmonary disease, or those living in settings with high HIV prevalence or high isoniazid resistance, should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for four months. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 13. Infants aged 0–3 months with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis should be promptly treated with standard treatment regimens as described in the above recommendations. Dose adjustments may be required to account for age and potential toxicity, and these decisions should be made by clinicians experienced in managing pediatric TB. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty of evidence. 14. During the continuation phase of treatment, thrice-weekly regimens may be considered for children who are not HIV-infected and are living in settings with well-established directly observed therapy. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 15. Streptomycin should not be used as part of first-line treatment regimens for children with pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. 16. Children with suspected or confirmed tuberculous meningitis or osteoarticular TB should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for ten months, for a total treatment duration of 12 months. The dosages for tuberculous meningitis are the same as those for pulmonary TB. This is a strong recommendation with low certainty of evidence.
